analysis.one_liner: Requires farm employers to protect workers from wildfire smoke and dangerous heat with respirators, water, shade, and rest breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate HELP Committee since its July 2025 introduction with no action, one cosponsor, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require farm employers to protect their workers from two growing dangers: wildfire smoke and extreme heat. Employers would have to provide respirators when the air becomes hazardous, water and cooling when the heat becomes dangerous, mandatory rest breaks in shaded or cleaner air, and training in a language workers understand. The Labor Department would have to write a permanent, enforceable standard within months, at least as strict as any state's rules. The bill has only been referred to a Senate committee and has gone no further.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2 million farmworkers and other agricultural employees who work outdoors through wildfire smoke and heat waves. The bill would give them N95 or N100 respirators when air quality turns dangerous, water and cooling facilities and shaded rest breaks when heat turns dangerous, and training in a language they understand [S2]. It would also protect them from being fired for asserting these rights, through the same anti-retaliation rules that apply to other workplace safety standards [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill takes effect immediately upon enactment by making an 'initial standard' legally enforceable right away: employers must provide NIOSH-certified N95 or N100 respirators when workplace air quality reaches a dangerous level, and require their use when it becomes extremely dangerous [S2].
It requires employers to provide water, cooling facilities, and other heat protections, with mandatory use when heat reaches an extremely dangerous level [S2].
Once air quality or heat hits a dangerous threshold, farmworkers must get rest breaks of at least 10 minutes every two hours in shaded areas with reduced smoke or temperature exposure [S2].

Employers must train workers, in a language they understand, on how to use the equipment, how long it works, and the health effects of smoke and heat, with a chance to ask questions; the Labor Department must develop sample materials, including in indigenous languages, and help hard-to-reach workers through community organizations [S2].

Within 90 days the Labor Department must begin writing a permanent standard at least as protective as any state's smoke or heat standard, and the initial standard is enforced like any OSHA rule, including protection against retaliation for workers who assert these rights [S2].
The bill's findings note that wildfire season has grown by over two months since the 1970s and that more than 100 people died in Oregon's June 2021 heat wave, including a farmworker [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers would pay the cost: buying and maintaining N95 or N100 respirators, providing water, shade, and cooling facilities, granting paid rest breaks of at least 10 minutes every two hours once conditions turn dangerous, and training workers in languages they understand [S2]. Enforcement would follow the normal Occupational Safety and Health Act process, including fines for violations [S2].

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on agricultural employers, who would face new expenses for respirators, water, cooling, shaded break areas, and training, and critics of federal heat rules argue these requirements are costly and difficult to run on farms with dispersed outdoor crews; the bill acknowledges cost concerns by offering employers free technical assistance and sample training materials from the Labor Department [S2].

The initial standard's trigger points are left to the Labor Secretary to define ('a level determined by the Secretary'), so the real-world strictness of the rules depends on how a future administration sets and enforces those thresholds [S2].
The bill covers only farmworkers employed by agricultural operations, leaving out other outdoor workers such as construction and delivery workers who face the same smoke and heat hazards.

Requiring respirators is a partial fix: N95 masks are hard to wear through a full shift of heavy labor in heat, which is why the bill pairs them with rest breaks rather than treating them as a complete answer [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are protections against two documented, life-threatening hazards for a workforce that has none at the federal level: respirators in wildfire smoke, water and shade in heat waves, and paid rest breaks when conditions turn dangerous [S2]. The costs are real but modest by workplace-safety standards: equipment, water and shade stations, and training, with the bill cushioning small employers through free Labor Department assistance and model materials [S2]. The main design weakness is that the danger thresholds are left to the Secretary's discretion, so the standard's bite depends on the administration in power [S2]. The larger obstacle is not the design but the bill's near-total lack of congressional support: it has one cosponsor and has not moved since referral [S3][S4].

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate health and labor committee the day it was introduced and has not moved since, so nothing has happened yet.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 31, 2025 and, the same day, was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action has been taken: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion activity appears in the record.
Only one senator cosponsored the bill, Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont, alongside sponsor Sen. Jeff Merkley.
Because Congress is still in session, the bill remains alive on paper but is dormant in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers are better off so far, because no new federal equipment, water, shade, or rest-break requirements have taken effect. Farmworkers remain without a federal heat and smoke standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural employers avoiding new safety costs

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal smoke and heat safety standard for farmworkers.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action on it; no markup or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: With only two Democratic senators involved and no Republican cosponsors, no roll-call has occurred, but the bill's one-chamber, one-party support matches the usual pattern for workplace-safety mandates.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (fruit, vegetable, and field-crop growers and farm labor contractors)
industries.note: The bill would make these employers pay for respirators, water, cooling facilities, shaded rest breaks, and multilingual training for their workforces [S2]. Agricultural employers have historically resisted federal heat and smoke rules as costly compliance burdens, so their interest in this bill runs against the workers it protects.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor, no action beyond referral to the HELP Committee since July 2025, and no scheduled markup, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Bills at this stage with this level of support almost always die quietly at the end of the Congress unless they pick up cosponsors or committee attention, neither of which has happened [S1][S3][S4].
